nameStory: The oak bracket gets its name from its shelf-like growth pattern that juts out from oak trees like a wooden bracket or shelf. 'Bracket fungus' is the common term for any mushroom that grows horizontally from tree trunks, and this species has a particular fondness for oak trees. The scientific name 'dryadeus' refers to dryads, the tree nymphs of Greek mythology who were said to live within oak trees.
description: The oak bracket is a large, woody shelf fungus that grows directly from the trunks of oak trees. These impressive fungi can reach over a foot across and have a thick, hoof-like appearance when viewed from the side. The upper surface is typically brown to rusty-brown with a bumpy, crusty texture, while the underside features tiny pores instead of gills. As a parasitic fungus, it slowly weakens its host tree over many years, often indicating that the oak is in decline.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Thick, hoof-shaped brackets that are brown to rusty-brown on top with a crusty, bumpy surface that feels rough like tree bark. Often develops concentric ridges or zones as it ages.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underside has tiny round pores (not gills) that are cream to pale brown when young, darkening to rusty-brown with age. The pore surface may weep orange-brown droplets when fresh.

idTips.label: Host Tree
idTips.description: Always grows directly from living oak trees, typically emerging from the base of the trunk or major roots. Never found on the ground or on other tree species.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Rock-hard and woody when mature, but younger specimens may have softer margins. The bracket feels heavy and solid, like a piece of wood rather than a typical mushroom.

idTips.label: Droplets
idTips.description: Fresh specimens often 'weep' amber to orange-brown droplets from the pore surface, especially in humid conditions. These droplets dry to leave dark stains.

habitat: Found exclusively on living oak trees throughout New England's forests, parks, and suburban areas where oaks are present. Most commonly appears at the base of mature oak trunks or emerging from large surface roots. Prefers older, stressed oak trees and is often one of the first signs that a seemingly healthy oak is actually in decline.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as small, soft bumps on oak trunks. Fresh brackets may show active weeping of orange droplets as temperatures warm and humidity increases.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with brackets expanding rapidly. Fresh margins are most noticeable now, often appearing lighter colored and softer than the older, crusty center portions.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows but brackets remain prominent and easy to spot. The weeping droplets are less common, and the surface becomes increasingly hard and crusty.
seasonality.winter: Brackets persist through winter as hard, woody shelves. Snow and ice may accumulate on the upper surfaces, making them even more noticeable against dark oak bark.

funFact: Oak brackets can live for decades on the same tree, adding new layers of growth each year like tree rings - some specimens have been aged at over 50 years old, slowly growing larger while their host oak gradually weakens and eventually dies.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with artist's bracket (Ganoderma applanatum), but artist's bracket grows on many tree species and has a white pore surface that bruises brown when scratched. Remember: oak bracket is oak-specific and weeps orange droplets, while artist's bracket is found on various trees and can be 'drawn' on with a fingernail.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'oak bracket,' this fungus is actually a tree pathogen that causes white rot in the heartwood of oaks. Finding this fungus on an oak tree is often bad news for the tree's long-term health, as it indicates internal decay that may not be visible from the outside.
compareHints: As the only Pseudoinonotus species in New England, oak bracket is most similar to other bracket fungi in the family Hymenochaetaceae. However, it's distinguished from relatives like Phellinus species by its exclusive relationship with oak trees and its distinctive orange droplet weeping. Unlike the flatter, more shelf-like Phellinus brackets, oak bracket tends to be thicker and more hoof-shaped in profile.
